paras: The lynching of Ned Clark was the shooting of a Black man, described in the press as "colored," by the men holding him prisoner in Worth County, Georgia, reported on June 26, 1888. Clark had been charged with attempting to assault a thirteen-year-old girl, and his captors said he was shot while trying to escape as they took him toward Irwin County; his body was found with nineteen bullets in it. The account, which came from a single dispatch out of Albany, ran in papers across the country and put Clark's name on a year-end list of the "Victims of Judge Lynch."

Clark was charged with attempting to assault a girl thirteen years of age, and several versions, including those in the Savannah Morning News and the Atlanta Constitution, described her as white and the charge as attempted rape. The alleged offense took place in Irwin County, which the dispatch called "the scene of his crime." A German-language summary in the Illinois Staats-Zeitung of Chicago stated the charge as an accomplished act and said Clark had been caught by "Bürgern" (citizens) in Worth County. None of the reports names the girl or the men who caught Clark.

According to a special dispatch from Albany to the Atlanta Constitution, relayed from Atlanta on June 26, news of the lynching reached Albany that day. Clark's captors had been conveying him to Irwin County, and they returned without him, saying that he had tried to escape in the woods and had been shot down. His body was then found with nineteen bullets in it, and the bushes around it were "riddled with balls." The reports give no number for the captors and do not say whether any of them held office.

No report of an inquest, an arrest or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage, which ends in Georgia with the Constitution's roundup of July 3. In late December the True Northerner of Paw Paw, Michigan, entered "Ned Clark in Worth County, Georgia" under June 26 in its annual roll of lynching victims, beside William Moore of Mattoon, Illinois.

The story traveled as wire copy datelined Atlanta, and the Savannah Morning News ran it under "Lynching in Worth" with the subhead "Ned Clark Shot to Death by His Captors." Other papers headlined the same text by the charge against him: the Memphis Appeal called it "A Rapist Shot Down," and the San Antonio Daily Light "Another Rapist Meets His Doom." Plainer heads included "A Negro Lynched" in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette and "Shot Down in the Georgia Woods" in the Hocking Sentinel of Logan, Ohio.

Shorter versions in the Salt Lake Herald, the Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union kept only the lynching and the charge. The Washington Evening Star paired it with the jail lynching of William Moore in Illinois under the heading "Two Lynchings," as did the Salt Lake Herald under "Lynched." In Elko, Nevada, the Daily Independent set the Clark item just above a note on Moore that ended "Swift, correct and cheap justice," a remark aimed at the Illinois case. Weekly news summaries in Wisconsin, Minnesota and Arizona cut the story to a single sentence as late as July 5.

Some versions dropped the word "white" from the description of the girl, but none questioned the captors' explanation that Clark died trying to escape. A week after the event the Atlanta Constitution repeated the captors' account in its "Through Dixie" roundup of Georgia news, beside an item noting that no lynching had been attempted in a separate rape charge at Roswell Junction.

One telegraphic brief placed the lynching in "Washington county, Georgia," while every other version, including the Albany special, names Worth County. Most dispatches give the date as June 26, though the Silver State's Atlanta item, dated June 27, said Clark was lynched "to day." How Clark died rests only on his captors' statement that he was shot while escaping.

Clark was shot dead by the men holding him on a charge of attempted assault, and the papers uniformly call it a lynching (A1, A2, A16); the captors are plural and the body had nineteen bullets, but no report gives their number (A1, A3).

All versions, including the Constitution's own roundup and the German brief, derive from one Albany special to the Atlanta Constitution relayed by wire (A2, A16, A15); no independent local account was found.
